verses.text: In those days there was no king in Israel. In those days the tribe of the Danites sought an inheritance to dwell in; for to that day, their inheritance had not fallen to them among the tribes of Israel.

The children of Dan sent five men of their family from their whole number, men of valor, from Zorah, and from Eshtaol, to spy out the land, and to search it. They said to them, “Go, explore the land!” They came to the hill country of Ephraim, to the house of Micah, and lodged there.

When they were by the house of Micah, they knew the voice of the young man the Levite; so they turned aside there, and said to him, “Who brought you here? What do you do in this place? What do you have here?”
He said to them, “Thus and thus has Micah dealt with me, and he has hired me, and I am become his priest.”
They said to him, “Please ask counsel of God, that we may know whether our way which we go shall be prosperous.”
The priest said to them, “Go in peace. Your way in which you go is before Yahweh.”

Then the five men departed, and came to Laish, and saw the people who were there, how they lived in safety, in the way of the Sidonians, quiet and secure; for there was no one in the land, possessing authority, that might put them to shame in anything, and they were far from the Sidonians, and had no dealings with anyone else.
They came to their brothers at Zorah and Eshtaol; and their brothers asked them, “What do you say?”
They said, “Arise, and let us go up against them; for we have seen the land, and behold, it is very good. Do you stand still? Don’t be slothful to go and to enter in to possess the land.
When you go, you will come to an unsuspecting people, and the land is large; for God has given it into your hand, a place where there is no lack of anything that is in the earth.”
The family of the Danites set out from Zorah and Eshtaol, with six hundred men armed with weapons of war.
They went up and encamped in Kiriath Jearim, in Judah. Therefore they called that place Mahaneh Dan, to this day. Behold, it is behind Kiriath Jearim.
They passed from there to the hill country of Ephraim, and came to the house of Micah.

Then the five men who went to spy out the country of Laish answered, and said to their brothers, “Do you know that there is in these houses an ephod, and teraphim,  and an engraved image, and a molten image? Now therefore consider what you have to do.”
They turned aside there, and came to the house of the young Levite man, even to the house of Micah, and asked him how he was doing.
The six hundred men armed with their weapons of war, who were of the children of Dan, stood by the entrance of the gate.

The five men who went to spy out the land went up, and came in there, and took the engraved image, the ephod, the teraphim, and the molten image; and the priest stood by the entrance of the gate with the six hundred men armed with weapons of war.
When these went into Micah’s house, and took the engraved image, the ephod, the teraphim, and the molten image, the priest said to them, “What are you doing?”

They said to him, “Hold your peace, put your hand on your mouth, and go with us, and be to us a father and a priest. Is it better for you to be priest to the house of one man, or to be priest to a tribe and a family in Israel?”
The priest’s heart was glad, and he took the ephod, the teraphim, and the engraved image, and went with the people.
So they turned and departed, and put the little ones, the livestock, and the goods before them.
When they were a good way from the house of Micah, the men who were in the houses near Micah’s house gathered together and overtook the children of Dan.
As they cried to the children of Dan, they turned their faces, and said to Micah, “What ails you, that you come with such a company?”
He said, “You have taken away my gods which I made, and the priest, and have gone away! What more do I have? How can you ask me, ‘What ails you?’”
The children of Dan said to him, “Don’t let your voice be heard among us, lest angry fellows fall on you, and you lose your life, with the lives of your household.”
The children of Dan went their way; and when Micah saw that they were too strong for him, he turned and went back to his house.

They took that which Micah had made, and the priest whom he had, and came to Laish, to a people quiet and unsuspecting, and struck them with the edge of the sword; then they burned the city with fire.
There was no deliverer, because it was far from Sidon, and they had no dealings with anyone else; and it was in the valley that lies by Beth Rehob. They built the city, and lived in it.
They called the name of the city Dan, after the name of Dan their father, who was born to Israel; however the name of the city used to be Laish.

The children of Dan set up for themselves the engraved image; and Jonathan, the son of Gershom, the son of Moses, and his sons were priests to the tribe of the Danites until the day of the captivity of the land.
So they set up for themselves Micah’s engraved image which he made, and it remained all the time that God’s house was in Shiloh.

footnotes.content: A king would have settled disputes justly; without one, each tribe scrambles for what it thinks it deserves. How easy it is to justify taking when no one's watching closely. The Spirit whispers: even our unanswered questions don't give us leave to run ahead.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zorah and Eshtaol were in Dan's original lot (Josh 19:41), yet they still scout. Five brave men, sent to find what was already given—how often do we spy out territories the Lord has already deeded to us, afraid we won't find them on our own?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They recognize the young Levite's voice—a small thing, yet it speaks to familiarity and connection. But connection won't protect him when expediency calls. We meet our friends not knowing which of us will waver.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He's become Micah's priest through wages, not calling. A hired man serves the hand that feeds him, not truth. The Levite should have served God alone, but comfort has its pull.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They ask the Levite to inquire of God—as though a hired priest had access to divine counsel. When we choose convenience over integrity, we lose the very thing we claim to seek: true guidance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Go in peace"—words meant to comfort. But peace isn't a blessing to pronounce when one lacks true authority. How many times do we offer false assurance, wanting to be liked more than helpful?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Laish is quiet, unsuspecting, wealthy—a city marked for destruction not by the Lord, but by its own isolation and prosperity. The text shows us what the Danites see: opportunity. It shows us what the Lord sees: judgment brewing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The spies return with a report. But a report is only as good as the hands that act on it. These hands will act—not in faith, but in appetite.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Very good"—the land looks rich and defenseless. They speak urgently, pushing aside hesitation. The word "slothful" stings: to stay put looks like laziness when the eye sees gain ahead.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They claim God has given the land into their hand—but He has given it nothing. They are taking what is not theirs, then wrapping theft in the language of the Lord's favor.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Six hundred armed men set out from Zorah and Eshtaol—the very place they started from. They leave in numbers and weapons; they leave in desire. This is migration as conquest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They camp at Mahaneh Dan ("Camp of Dan"), and the name stuck. Places remember what people do in them. A name given in haste becomes a monument to haste.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They pass through Ephraim back to Micah's house. They've tasted conquest; now they want to harvest. The path back is always shorter than the first walk.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The ephod, teraphim, and idols—objects of false worship, yet they matter enough to steal. They'll carry these dead things north as though holy relics. We're often too clever in finding religious cover for our plunder.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They greet him casually—"How are you doing?"—as though nothing has changed. Betrayal often wears a smile.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Six hundred armed men stand at the gate, silent and waiting. This is how power speaks: quietly, with swords visible.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The theft is quick—five men slip in while the priest stands at the gate with six hundred behind him. He sees the army; he says nothing. That's the moment he chooses his side.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest asks, "What are you doing?"—but he already knows. The question hangs, polite and small, in the face of armed theft.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They silence him and offer him a promotion—from hired priest of one household to priest of a whole tribe. Ambition speaks sweetly; it offers us what we wanted all along. He never resists.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His heart was glad. That's the saddest word here—not anger, not fear, but gladness. He'd become a man who could be bought.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The procession moves: children, livestock, goods, idols, and a priest who has chosen his new masters. A whole tribe migrating, and no one asked whether the Lord had sent them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Micah's neighbors gather and pursue. They had no king and little power, but they had community—and they tried to stop the theft. Their failure is noble compared to the tribe's success.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "What ails you?" Micah cries out. The question is one of bewilderment—he doesn't see himself as the thief; he sees Dan as the thief. That's what envy does: it reverses the mirrors.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He grieves what he made as though it were sacred—"my gods which I made." His idols were never real; his loss reveals what he'd truly valued. We mourn most what we built with our own hands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Dan speaks: silence yourself or die. The hand that takes can destroy. Power has no conscience, and Micah understands it suddenly, when it's too late.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Micah turns back, alone. His pursuit had been just—to recover what was taken—but he was too small for the evil he'd opened the door to. His surrender is a lesson: we cannot undo theft by our own strength once it's past.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Laish falls suddenly—a people at peace murdered in the night, then burned. The city that looked like a prize became a grave. This is what taking looks like when the taking isn't the Lord's.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Far from Sidon, with no allies—Laish was isolated, which made it both tempting and defenseless. The geography here teaches: safety lies not in distance or strength, but in the Lord's keeping.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They renamed it Dan after their ancestor—a land renamed is a land claimed. But the text remembers: it used to be Laish. Names can be changed; truth remains.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan, son of Moses, became their priest—a grandson of Moses, yet tending idols. His lineage couldn't protect him. The text marks this until "the day of captivity," when false worship finally fell. Generations of wrong ends in exile.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo: Micah's carved image stayed put through the years, outlasting empires, until the Lord swept it away. We build idols we think will last forever, then wonder where they went when He moves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
